intro: Segmentation maps contain class IDs, not intensities. Resizing must select existing labels rather than interpolate between their numeric values.
task: Resize an integer label map with the documented nearest-neighbor coordinate rule.
requirements: labels is a height-by-width matrix of integer IDs 0..1000000. output_size is a two-entry integer vector with values 1..64.

Return output[i,j]=labels[floor(i*input_height/output_height),floor(j*input_width/output_width)] as an integer matrix. This uses asymmetric floor coordinates, not align-corners or half-pixel rounding.

Use finite real numeric values of magnitude at most 1e6, excluding boolean inputs. Each array axis has 1..64 entries and at most 65536 elements total unless a stricter bound is stated. Return NumPy arrays for array outputs, preserve caller inputs, and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Double both axes
examples.output:
[[1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 1, 2, 2], [3, 3, 4, 4], [3, 3, 4, 4]]
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

hints.title: Follow the data
hints.body: Construct source indices independently for the two output axes.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: Never average class identifiers, even when downsampling.

explanation: Nearest-neighbor selection preserves the set of available class labels. It is appropriate when numeric distances between label IDs have no meaning.

Different nearest-neighbor coordinate conventions can disagree at boundaries. Naming this floor mapping makes the operation reproducible and prevents accidental comparison with a different library convention.
